en: An Exposition on the Verses Defining the Characteristics of Stūpas, including the Characteristics of Miscellaneous Caityas.
The work of the Master Bhadravyūha, belonging to the Noble Lokottaravādins; Sphuṭārthā, p. 208.
Success! Homage to the Buddha!
Whatever has been taught in the *Prakīrṇaka-vinaya* by the Lokottaravādins, and whatever characteristics of a stūpa are found in the sūtras and other texts of other schools; (1)
The Lord of the World has shown this little by little here and there; all of it is now being told here by Bhadrayūha as if it were a bridge.
One should have it constructed on a portion of ground that is accessible, pure as a building site, not unstable, elevated like the sky, smooth, and clean. // 3 //
It is declared to be one yojana in height and half a yojana in circumference; the railing is one krośa wide, as stated in the *Prakīrṇaka-vinaya*.
The height of the stūpa is proclaimed to be equal to the circumference of the dome;
from that same proportion, the rim and so forth, up to the top of the central shaft, are established in succession.
The rim at the bottom should be square, and it should also be made with a width equal to half that [of the rim] and joined to the measurement of the basket.
The rim should be fashioned at one-eighth the height of the bowl;
it is traditionally taught that the cleansing of the ground should continue until the rising water becomes pure.
It should be raised by one-eighth [of its width], with the rim made according to the required measure;
the mandala may be circular or square, or otherwise fashioned accordingly.
Above that, altars (vedikās) should be constructed, numbering four, three, two, or one;
they may be quadrangular, octagonal, or circular. // 9 //
One should construct a raised altar joined with the sacrificial hall on one side,
adorned on all sides of the casket with various sciences.
Therefore, in the four corner sections, three [lines] should be drawn according to the measurement of the central square; the fourth is the image (biṃba). 11.
The text breaks off here,
as folio 2a and 2b are missing. From the commentary:
I quote the fragmentary portions of the verses contained in the textual section of folios 2a and 2b:
*adhaś caturthake bhāge ... [12] (§16.6a.2).
*bāhyakoṣṭha ṣaḍ āyāmety ādi ... [13] (§17.6a.4–5).*
"Thus, for those whose sequence is not exhausted... [14] (§17.6a.7).
"The width below the altar is made equal to that of the short side of the altar... [15] (§18.6b.7). "One should act likewise by raising [the height]," and so forth. [16] (§19.7a.l).
"Three altars," such as the "shank-altar" (*jaṅghā-vedikā*) and so forth—this is to be supplied [to the text].
"It should not emerge like a reflection," and so forth.
"For [the image] has risen within a casket," and so forth.
And then, from the *Karaṇḍa*, [it says]: "Turmeric," thus [20] (§21.7a.7).
"The egg should be wrapped," thus [21] (§22.7b.1).
"Below that, of the outer compartment" [22] (§23.7b.2).
"Having the shape of that bowl, peaceful" [22a] (§23.7b.3).
"Completely equal to the mind, gentle," and so forth [23] (§23.7b.5).
"Beyond that, of the outer square," and so forth.
"The twenty-five squares," and so forth.
Four types of persons (*pudgala*) are recognized.
The Arhat, the Wheel-turning King, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Victor are each a Victor. // 26 //
For those in training (śaikṣas), for Arhats, for the Solitary Conqueror (khaḍgajina), and for the Victor (jina), a row of parasols adorned with one additional [parasol] should be fashioned. // 27 //
Within the body, it is endowed with the elements, yet devoid of the dharma-element;
it consists of the uṣṇīṣa, the moon, the sun, the pillars, and the two bells. (28)
One should describe the intrinsic nature of this stūpa, beginning with its base and proceeding in sequence up to its summit. (29)
Śikṣāsamuccaya §3:
1. Generosity is the earth; 2. Ethical discipline is the rim.
3. The four noble lineages are the courtyards;
4. the four noble truths are the stairways; 5. the grounds of self-confidence are the pillars.
6. The foundations of mindfulness are the lower altar; 7. the right efforts are the second altar. (Slkv p.
8. The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the third terrace;
9. the five faculties (*indriya*) beginning with faith are the fourth, the shank-terrace;
10. the five powers (*bala*) beginning with faith are the neck.
11. The Dharma-gates of impermanence and so forth are the four flower-holders.
12. The untainted pliancy born of the stage of the first dhyāna is the neck-ornament (*kaṇṭhaka*) of the awakening-factor of pliancy.
13. That which is born of the stages of the second and third dhyānas—the joy and rapture—is the necklace (*kaṇṭhakavalaya*) and the torque (*valitaka*) of the awakening-factor of joy.

14. The feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) arising from the stages of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the fourth dhyāna, and so forth, is the factor of awakening of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*); it is the *harmikā*.

15. The factors of awakening of mindfulness (*smṛti*), investigation of phenomena (*dharma-pravicaya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*) are the four world-protectors (*lokapāla*). (Slkv p. 212)
16. The Noble Eightfold Path is the staff;
17. the powers of one whose outflows are exhausted, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and the thirteen parasols are the banners;
18. the uṣṇīṣa is the purity of great compassion. (Bénisti)
Above that, through the purification of supreme great compassion, is the *uṣṇīṣa*.
(19) The stainless realm of nirvāṇa is the white parasol.
*Slkv* p. 213.
20. Conventional truth and ultimate truth; the moon and the sun. 21. These two verses on the Noble Jewel are the two bells pertaining to the self within the sphere of sentient beings.
22. The knowledge of all modes is the parasol.
23. "The banner of the liberation of the mind whose nature is non-attachment"—thus [begins] that Blessed One, and so forth.
24. The section on the characteristics of the scattered caityas, known as the "Banners of Glory," is completed.
This is the work of the Master Bhadravyūha, an adherent of the noble Lokottaravāda school.
*Śataśāstra-vṛtti-kārikā*, p. 214, §4.
Victorious are the Blessed Tathāgatas, who have conquered all faults, attained the summit of all virtues, and overcome the cycle of birth. // 1 //
I bow my head in homage to that ascetic named Bhadravyūha, who, by means of his instructions, constructed a stūpa for the benefit of the world. // 2 //

In order to bring about correct understanding for those whose minds are characterized by doubt or misconception regarding the command, the analysis of the treatise on the characteristics of the stūpa is here set forth. (3)
*Sūtrālaṃkāravṛttibhāṣya* §5: "The section on miscellaneous topics," and so forth.
The salutation to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) is for the sake of following the practice of the virtuous.
For what purpose did the Teacher begin with this salutation?
For the teacher has already performed the salutation at the beginning of the *Prakīrṇavinayasaṃgraha-kārikā* and other works:
"To that Sage whose speech, mind, and body are in every way incomparable."
"Having abandoned that, I shall speak the *Vinayakārikā*, which is the essence of continuity."
And since this [portion] is but a part of that [work], it is not explicitly stated here by the word "iti.
For this very reason, the author of the treatise indicates its existence through the phrase "the *Prakīrṇaka-vinaya*," and so forth; therefore, there is no fault.
For in the *Prakīrṇaka*, that which was [spoken] by the Blessed One Kāśyapa during the time when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years—[namely] the *Kṛkī-sūtra*...
The king constructed a stūpa one yojana in height and one yojana in circumference, with a base extending half a yojana and a railing one krośa in height.
Having displayed it made of copper, iron, and brass for him to touch by hand, he said:
"When constructing or having a stūpa built on a level site, the enclosure wall must be made in this manner."
Slkv §7: Now, the courtyard (aṅgaṇa), the altar (vedī), the base (jaṅghā), the flower-holder (puṣpagrahaṇīya),

the neck-base (yakā), the dome (aṇḍaka), the neck-ring (kaṇṭhaka), the small neck-ring (kaṇṭhikā), the terrace (harmikā), the series of parasols (chatrāvalī), the parasol (chatra), the bell (ghaṇṭā), the banner (dhvaja), the flag (patākā), the stūpa-house (stūpagṛha), the scripture (āgama), the lotus pond (puṣkiriṇī), and the enclosure wall (prākāra) have been described.
Furthermore, regarding the miscellaneous connection, this was not stated [there]:

"When I was a universal monarch (cakravartin), I built a stūpa one yojana high and one yojana in circumference. That [statement] is found in the *Stūpakalpanāsūtra* and in the *Kṣudraka* of other schools, namely the Sarvāstivādins.

In the *Sragdharāstotra* (Slkv), section 8, it is stated that there is a stūpa containing relics, a pillar, four surrounding assemblies, a pillar with stairs, world-protectors, and the presence of the moon, white garments, banners, the dolphin-bannered god (Kāmadeva), and so forth.
Furthermore, in the *Kūṭāgārasūtra*, it is said:
"For the sake of even a relic the size of a mustard seed, one should construct a stūpa the size of an āmalaka fruit."
In that stūpa, one should erect a staff even as thin as a needle,
and place a parasol even as small as a jujube leaf;
having approached it, thus it is said.
In a place that is accessible, praiseworthy, and frequented by many people— or even if it is not—
where the site is pure and possesses the characteristics prescribed by the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā),
and which is not already occupied or devoid of other shrines (caityas).

One should not eat on ground that is devoid of elevation, nor on ground that is elevated in the center, nor on ground that is greasy, nor on ground that is dry, nor on ground that is impure, nor on ground that is defiled by filth.
Having thus determined the specific location for the emergence of the stūpa, he speaks while demonstrating its characteristics, beginning with "by the circumference of the dome" (*kumbhasya*).
*Parihana* means circumference (*pariṇāha*). *Pariṇāha*.
The circumference of the middle part is the girth-band, like a man endowed with height and circumference.
And in that context, height is expressed by the word *āroha*,
not by the word *pariṇāha*; for height is denoted by the word *pariṇāha*.
Likewise here as well, by the word "circumference" (*pariṇāha*), the encircling of the central thread in the four directions around the circular navel is intended,
according to the analogy of the spokes of a wheel.
The fourth [case] also applies to objects situated in vessels and so forth, because that measure of width is invariably present there.
What is the point of this relative circumference? The meaning is that the stūpa’s length is desired to be equal to the circumference of the *kumbha* (the dome) or the *karaṇḍaka* (the harmikā).
For it is stated in the *Prakīrṇaka-vinaya*: "It should be one *yojana* in height and one *yojana* in circumference," and so forth, beginning with "The rim (*nemi*) should be square."
The meaning is that on the square ground, the jar (kumbha) and the basket (karaṇḍa) have a circumference corresponding to the proportions of the mandala.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Prakīrṇaka*:

"One who is having a stūpa constructed should have it built up to the edge of the enclosure wall. For the sake of following that sequence, here, from the laying of the lines for the square mandala, there is an encircling of the central compartment both internally and externally.
And on the interior side,
it should be understood according to the system of eighty-one squares;
furthermore, within that, it should be seen as having a width equal to half the thickness of the rim-wall (nemi-bhitti).
"By one-eighth of the *karaṇḍaka*" and so forth means that the smoothing (*nimarjana*) should be done below the rim (*nemi*) by one-eighth of the circumference of the jar (*kumbha*);
the meaning is that it should extend either as far as the water breaks out or until the ground is purified.
"Raised by one-eighth part" and so forth means that having taken one-eighth from the measurement of the rim, the raised portion should be made by means of that; such is the meaning.
For it is said in the *Prakīrṇaka*:
"O lady, one must not occupy the space above.
However, in detail, it is desired that [the pillar] extends beyond the altar by a foot equal to the circumference of the *kumbha*.
"A square sacrificial post, a square altar, and an altar with recessed sides should be made.
Thus it is stated in the Āgamas of the Sarvāstivādins:
"The four [sides] should be made even; [the measurements are] four, three, two, and one."
By the phrase "one by number," a connection is made with the altars: four altars are to be constructed;
the first altar consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Up to the five sense-faculties, the fourth is the altar (vedī).
By this very rule, the reality of the altars has been stated.
[Ślokavārttika §15] What kind of connection with shape (saṃsthāna) is being made?
Regarding this, it is said: "Whether four-cornered, eight-cornered, or circular"—referring to the passage beginning with "all [the houses] joined as one," and so forth.
One should consider the vessels for receiving the incoming flowers.
The meaning is that one should make the fourth [section] from the pedestal of the legs (*jaṅghāvedikā*). For it is stated in the *Prakīrṇaka*:
"In the four directions, openings (*āyaka*) should be made."
"These images of the Buddha should be installed here;
a flower-gathering [ceremony] should be performed.
In this context, the word *āyaka* refers to the protector.

By the term "Flower-Receiver" (*puṣpagrahaṇī*), it is meant that outside the altar, or all around it, there is an arrangement of statues representing previous births, arranged in the form of rows of ponds and consisting merely of house-doors of various shapes.
Regarding the passage in the *Ślokavārttika* beginning with "in the lower four-cornered portion" (*adhaś catuskoṇake bhāge*) and so forth:
taking the *harmikā* as the reference point, that which is the fourth outer square-section below it is there [to be understood] as being made from a heap of grain,
by means of the entire fourth section.
With three parts it has the shape of a vessel;
with two parts it has the shape of a bird's beak;
and with one part it has the shape of a jar.
"Of the size of the middle square" means by means of the measurement starting from the size of the middle square, and so forth.
This is what is meant:
there too, by means of the division of parts, [the shape] of the heap of grain [is formed].
Three altars (vedīs) should be made according to the measurement of the middle section; for the remaining ones, however, it is according to their respective proportions.
The fourth is "for the viewing of the image" (bimbapaśyaka), which means in accordance with the placement of the water-pot (kumbha).
This is what is intended.

In the lower fourth part of the three altars that have been constructed, there is the measure of the fourth leg-altar (*jaṅghā-vedī*), which consists of four squares; the meaning is that it is situated in the positions of the *kumbha* [mouldings].
As it is stated in the *Prakīrṇaka*:

"Jaṅghāpuṭavedī kukṣitavyā" means that the *puṭavedī* (folded altar) belongs to the shank; thus, it is the *jaṅghāpuṭavedī*. Alternatively, the *puṭavedī* is connected to the shank, meaning that the *kumbha* (vase) is adorned with lotus scrolls.
*Śulvasūtra* §17: "The external square has six spans," and so forth.
One should construct the lower altar (*adhovedī*) with a width equal to the extent of the six external squares—that is, its length should be that long.

Now, since it is stated that the altar (*vedikā*) is [measured] by the external square, one whose length is delimited by the number six should fashion the lower altar to the measure of exactly six spans of the external square.
Since it is stated in the *Prakīrṇaka* that for a [stūpa] one *yojana* high, the altar (*vedi*) is only one *krośa*,
therefore [the phrase] "those following the sequence of others" refers to the three altars situated above the height of the lower altar.
One should construct them in sequence according to the measurement of the central square; or alternatively, because of the statement that "four [squares] should be made surrounding [it]."
Like the terraces of Mount Meru, one should conceive of the height as increasing by half and half again;
thus has the stūpa situated on the ground been described. Now, regarding the stūpa constructed upon a leveled site:
The meaning is that [the stability] arises precisely from the mountain of mental construction (*kalpanācala*).
It is said that this brings about the nourishment of steadfastness (*sthairya*).
Therefore, showing the cause for the cleansing by means of the earth (*bhūmi*), he says:
In the case of *vetsyā* and so forth, it is equal;

however, this [measurement] is for the purpose of wiping—that is, for the purpose of cleaning the ground around the stūpa. As for the reduction [of measurement] from the height of the stūpa, it is for the sake of leveling with the height of the stūpa; but for what purpose is the width of the platforms (*vedikā*) [measured]? It is for the purpose of making them level with the height of the stūpa.
For it is desired that the height of the stūpa be equal to its width at the base of the altar (vedī).
As it is stated in the *Mahāvastu*: "When I was a Cakravartin king, a stūpa was built by me one yojana in height and one yojana in width.
For in this case, just as in the case of a jar shaped like a heap of grain, once the yojanas have been established [as the dimensions], the designation of "one yojana" is understood.

Likewise, the stūpa is intended to be as high as the circumference of the dome (kumbha); the width at the base of the pedestal (vedi) is made equal to that of the pedestal. How, then, could there be an exceeding of the prescribed measurements?

Due to the power of the mental construction of the site, the measurement of the circumference of the courtyard is not exceeded by the measurement of the interior, because the form of the pitcher is small relative to the height of the altar;
thus, its immersion cannot be perceived.
As it is said: "One should act accordingly by raising [the vessel]," and so forth. (Ślokavārttika §19)
This is what is meant:

starting from the *harmikā*, that portion which was previously established for the outer fourth square-section below—that same division should be used for the three altars (*vedi*), beginning with the pillar-altar (*jaṅghā-vedikā*) and so forth;
one should understand that they must not protrude beyond [the base], just as the image [does not]. And so on.
*Sūksma-vinaya-kārikā* §20: When the rim has been formed by the flow of water,
or when the dwelling is small,
one should make the upper altar elevated so that the basket does not settle downward from the rim.
Once it has entered below, it is not fit to be placed back again.
"Emerging from the *karaṇḍaka*," and so forth.

By means of the fourth *jaṅghāvedi*, which is primarily directed upward, the emergence of the *kumbha* and its downward refinement are accomplished precisely through the process of its reduction and increase.
(Slkv p. 219)

The meaning of *Slkv* §21 is that since there is neither increase nor decrease in the three altars (*vedītraya*), one should therefore not [perform the rite] on a lower level; rather, one should do so from the short [measure] at the *kumbha*.
As for what he will state later:
The emergence of the jar depends solely upon its visible portion; for, in that case,
from the perspective of ultimate reality, only a mere depression or elevation is perceived,
and not the actual emergence of the jar or its sinking downward.
Then, having placed a casket containing musk upon a heap of grain or a similar structure situated over the *jaṅghāpuṭavedī*, one should fashion a round jar.
For it is stated in the *Prakīrṇa*:
"The egg [of the calculation] should be laid.
The two verses concerning the division of the grid, beginning with "divided ninefold," etc., are easy to understand.

Rising from the sacrificial seat measured by two external squares, it is circular, intended for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and shaped like a heap of grain; however, it is not three parts high, because it is a site sacred to Śiva (*śivasthala*).
*Ślokavārttika* §23: "Below that, of the outer square," and so forth.
Of that [mandala], there is an outer square consisting of half of a circular portion, measured by half [the size].
That which has arisen from the altar-seat (vedyāsana) measured by half of the outer square—
"Having the shape of that vessel for one desiring peace"—
that is,
even from that configuration of the vessel.
By that same intermediate measurement, from the seat measured by the outer square-cells,
that which arises is the "elevation-maker," which has the shape of an egg.
"Completely level and gentle," and so forth.

Having cast aside mere obsessive attachment, when one has arisen from the seats that are known through the upward measurements above the external chambers of the meditative absorption by means of the nature of pure being (*sattva*),
then [the rule] "it should not be done in the flower-caskets," and so forth, applies.
Śikṣāsamuccaya §24: Not only should an image of a Bodhisattva be made of gold with a water-pot, but an image of the Buddha as well;
for it is said in the *Prakīrṇaka*:
"A hundred thousand [pieces of gold]—this refers to the ornaments with which one should adorn a stūpa."
For where even the ornamenting of an image is prohibited, how could there be [permission] for the image itself?
This is because the Blessed One himself performed circumambulation of a stūpa out of compassion.

*Ślokavārttika* §25: "Then, above the outer box" (*tad ūrdhvaṃ bāhyakoṣṭhasya*) and so forth; by the elevation resulting from the removal of a portion of the outer box, there is the abandonment of the fourth half and the acceptance of the remaining three quarters. This is the elevation. Having divided that [height] into six parts, one half-part enters into the interior of the *kumbha*, while two parts constitute the *kaṇṭhaka*. One part is the *kaṇṭhikāvalitakā*, and the *harmikā* follows in due order. *Ślokavārttika* §26: One part is the *kaṇṭhikāvalitakā*, and the *harmikā* follows in due order.
The *harmikā* is one-eleventh of the increase in height, or half a part in its width;
its width is equal to the width of the outer chamber, and below it, a neck (*kaṇṭhaka*) is formed on all sides according to its own measurement.
One should make it diminished;
or otherwise one may arrange it according to what is beautiful.
This *sākārikā* [verse] is easy to understand.
*Ślokavārttika* §27: "Twenty-five compartments," and so forth.

By means of the division into twenty-five compartments, there is the grasping of the base, middle, and top of the sacrificial post (*yaṣṭi*). Above the *harmikā*, in the four locations shaped like water-pots (*kumbha*), the measurement of the two outer compartments extends downward as far as [the base].
The stūpa enters the heart-chamber;
for from the emergence of the heart-chamber, it proceeds in due order through the forms of the pinnacle-vase and so forth.
Just as one should understand that with the exhaustion of the length of a pillar, there is also the exhaustion of its circumference, so it is in this manner up to that point.
In the *Śilpa-prakaraṇa*, section 28, the characteristics, dimensions, and shape of the stūpa are well-expounded;
it should be made so that it is beautiful, without exceeding the stated characteristics and dimensions, and in its shape, by means of the projection of the dome (*prastā-kumbha*).
Having fashioned an image out of silver, gem, gold, stone, or wood,
in a fragrant location that is praiseworthy and beautiful,
[one should do so] with one's own hand or by the hand of a craftsman.
In that manner, one should perform the conceptualization with one's own intellect; for it has been said: "One should act in such a way that it may become beautiful."
"In this future time," because this treatise on the characteristics of stūpas presents merely the essential subject matter;
"by whatever merit has been acquired by me, let there be a stūpa for the Sugata, the person."
The analysis in the *Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā* is completed.
Following this is a note by a Nepalese librarian in the Newārī script:
Śrī Syaṅguyāyita Siyā Jetanaku 35 aṅgulī Ḍā 5 yavanhasa 7 saaṃkanaghāva. (Śrī Syaṅguyāyita Siyā Jetanaku 35 fingers, Ḍā 5, yavanhasa 7, with its own seal.)

The measurement of the middle and other parts in sequence is: nine *ghala-saku* and five *ku* for the *ghala-saku*; three *umaḍe* and eighteen *thaṃthu-ucaku* and five *aṃśu* for the *yavanhana*. Thus it is.
On the upper drawsheet,
there are the following lines:
1 x x x x x pralase tīsijya pu manasīyā tachosathu se kho thu teya u(?).
There is no shelter for them;
this is the Dharma, O disciple... [of the one who has gone beyond].
Immediately after that, having written the dharma, one should perform the ālepana.
An analysis of the *Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā*, year 2 of the Vudja era.
